extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent applicants/attorneys
extracted.subtask_short: patent enablement and best mode review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent specification satisfies the enablement (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph) and best mode requirements and related evidentiary issues (affidavits, prior art, arguments of counsel, utility). Intended to direct examiner practice and applicant responses during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer program disclosure sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures involving computer programs should include either the computer program itself or a reasonably detailed flowchart which delineates the sequence of operations the program must perform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the software disclosure only includes a flowchart, as the complexity of functions and the generality of components increase, the basis for challenging sufficiency becomes more reasonable because the likelihood of more than routine experimentation increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's burden after examiner raises reasonable basis of nonenablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Once USPTO personnel have advanced a reasonable basis or presented evidence to question the adequacy of a disclosure, the applicant must show that the specification would enable one of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the claimed invention without resorting to undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical applicant responses include submitting affidavits, referencing prior art patents or technical publications, presenting arguments of counsel, or combinations of these approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit practice — affiant skill level must match routineer
rubrics_metrics.description: Affiants should be of the person of ordinary skill in the art (the 'routineer'); an affiant whose skill level is higher or lower than that of the routineer may be challenged as not probative of the amount of experimentation required by a routineer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An affiant with higher skill would understate experimentation required; one with lower skill would overstate it. The affiant’s qualifications and relationship to the routineer should be analyzed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit practice — need for factual underpinning (not mere conclusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits that present conclusions on the ultimate legal question of sufficiency often fail if they contain few facts to support or buttress those conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits should provide factual evidence (e.g., number of programmers needed, man-hours, level of skill) rather than bare statements that features are 'well-known' or that a routineer 'could program' the system; affidavit evidence should reflect what was known at the time of filing to be probative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit timeliness/probativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit must be probative of the level of skill of the routineer as of the time the applicant filed the application; stating what was known when the affidavit was executed rather than at filing is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should critically analyze whether affidavits describe facts known at filing and whether the factual basis is sufficient to rebut a prima facie case of nonenablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referencing prior art documents — commercial availability and sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial availability of a prior art computer system is pertinent to enablement, but may not be sufficient to meet the applicant's burden by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely citing extracts from technical publications or prior art is insufficient unless it is made clear which parts of the cited material a skilled person would use and how components could be interconnected to produce the required results; less critical where components are essentially standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art patents must predate the application's effective filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art patents relied on by applicants to show the state of the art must have an issue date earlier than the effective filing date of the application under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents issued after the filing date are not evidence of subject matter known to persons skilled in the art for the purpose of enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration/interconnection of prior art components
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if enumerated devices or blocks are old, disclosure must make clear how they are interconnected to function in the claimed complex combination; otherwise undue experimentation is likely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must set forth the integration of the prior art; otherwise relying on old components does not demonstrate enablement for the combined system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of cited patents' relevance and level of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Cited patents used to demonstrate that particular hardware or software components are old must be analyzed as to whether they are germane to the instant invention and whether they provide better detail of disclosure than the applicant’s own disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A cited programming technique does not demonstrate that a skilled person could make and use the applicant's technique unless both are of approximately the same degree of complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments of counsel insufficient as substitute for evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments of counsel may be effective to show an examiner erred, but arguments alone cannot take the place of evidence once an examiner has advanced a reasonable basis to question the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the record consists substantially of attorney argument and opinion, factual affidavits or other evidence could be required to support the applicant’s position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between utility (35 U.S.C. 101) and enablement (35 U.S.C. 112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph requirement as to how to use the invention is different from the utility requirement under 35 U.S.C. 101, which requires some specific, substantial, and credible use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim may have credible utility yet still be defective under 35 U.S.C. 112 if one skilled in the art would have to engage in undue experimentation to practice the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner initial burden to show reasonable doubt of asserted utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner has the initial burden of challenging an asserted utility; only after the examiner provides evidence that a skilled person would reasonably doubt the asserted utility does the burden shift to the applicant to rebut.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections and factual showings are required before a 112 rejection grounded on lack of utility may be maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant rebuttal standard for asserted utility
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no predetermined amount or character of evidence an applicant must provide to support an asserted utility; the necessary character and amount will vary with the claim and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence is sufficient if, considered as a whole, it leads a person of ordinary skill in the art to conclude the asserted utility is more likely than not true; not required to be 'beyond a reasonable doubt.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement may be lacking even when utility is satisfied
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention can have a specific and substantial utility but still fail the enablement requirement if the specification does not teach how to effect that use without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph should be imposed separately from any rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101 for lack of utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement commensurate in scope with the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement is evaluated against the claimed subject matter; the focus is whether everything within the scope of the claim is enabled and whether the disclosure teaches how to make and use the full scope without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First determine exactly what subject matter the claims encompass (consider the claim as a whole), then determine if a skilled person is enabled to make and use that entire scope; scope of enablement must bear a reasonable correlation to scope of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims incorporate limitations (35 U.S.C. 112, fourth paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: When construing dependent claims, they shall be construed to incorporate by reference all limitations of the claim to which they refer and therefore further limit the subject matter claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must follow the fourth paragraph when considering dependent claims in enablement analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection for claims broader than enabling disclosure (first paragraph enablement rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 as broader than the enabling disclosure is an enablement (first paragraph) issue, not a definiteness (second paragraph) issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How teaching is set forth (specific example or broad terminology) is not determinative; the key is whether the disclosure enables the full claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single means claim undue breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: A single means claim (means recitation not in combination with other recited element of means) is subject to an undue breadth rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph if it covers every conceivable means for achieving the stated purpose while the specification discloses at most those means known to the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims have been held nonenabling where specification does not limit or disclose the full range of means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoperative embodiments and enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of inoperative embodiments within the scope of a claim does not necessarily render a claim nonenabled; the standard is whether a skilled person could determine which conceived-but-not-yet-made embodiments are operative with no more effort than normally required in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims reading on significant numbers of inoperative embodiments render claims nonenabled when the specification does not clearly identify operative embodiments and undue experimentation is involved in determining which embodiments are operative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical feature taught but not claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: A feature taught as critical in the specification and not recited in the claims should result in a rejection under the enablement provision of 35 U.S.C. 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In determining criticality, consider the entire disclosure; features that are merely preferred are not critical. Make an enablement rejection only when the specification language makes clear the limitation is critical for function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement — two-prong inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with the best mode requirement requires (1) a subjective inquiry whether, at filing, the inventor possessed a best mode for practicing the invention, and (2) an objective inquiry whether the written description disclosed that best mode so that a skilled person could practice it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All applicants are required to disclose for the claimed subject matter the best mode contemplated by the inventor even if the applicant was not the discoverer of that mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode — failure to disclose need not be extreme to be actionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to disclose the best mode need not rise to the level of active concealment or grossly inequitable conduct to support a rejection; omission of a specific material that would enable reproduction can violate the requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an inventor knows of a specific material that will make possible successful reproduction of claimed effects but only speaks in broad categories without disclosing that material, the best mode requirement may not be satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of AIA on best mode enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 15 of the AIA amended 35 U.S.C. 282 so that failure to disclose the best mode shall not be a basis on which any claim may be canceled or held invalid or otherwise unenforceable in litigation; however, the best mode requirement in 35 U.S.C. 112 remains for examination purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change affects post-issuance litigation remedies but does not alter patent examining practices for evaluating best mode in applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations relevant to best mode (practical points)
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing best mode: determine what the invention is (claims define it); a specific working example is not required; designation as 'best mode' is not required; updating best mode is not required; a defect in best mode cannot be cured by adding new matter after filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification need not set forth details unrelated to the essence of the invention; best mode may be a preferred range or group of reactants; proposed amendments adding an undisclosed best mode are new matter and should be objected to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode is distinct from enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The best mode provision of 35 U.S.C. 112 is separate and distinct from the enablement requirement; best mode is not directed merely to the absence of any mode (which would be nonenablement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess best mode and enablement separately during examination.
